title: Macmillan Staff Say the Publisher Threw a Party for a Workplace AI Assistant That Was Later Killed
gist: Wired reports that Macmillan staff say the publisher celebrated its internal AI assistant NOA with a launch party in January 2024 and then saw Chaptr sunset it in October 2025, while Big Five staff and authors describe executive pressure to adopt AI and growing author backlash.

insights.claim: Macmillan launched NOA, an AI chatbot from Chaptr (backed by parent Holtzbrinck), with a staff party in January 2024, but employees say it was unhelpful and unreliable and Chaptr announced its sunset in October 2025.
insights.speaker: Adam Morgan
insights.so_what: A heavily promoted enterprise AI assistant failed to earn adoption; evidence of the gap between rollout hype and actual use.
insights.quote: It was terrible, and no one used it,

insights.claim: Staff were told NOA was a closed environment where proprietary information could be input without sharing data with third parties, yet were also warned it could hallucinate and must always be fact-checked by humans.
insights.speaker: Adam Morgan
insights.so_what: Vendor data-privacy assurances and hallucination caveats coexisted; watch how enterprises govern manuscripts in AI tools.
insights.locator: Macmillan staffers say they were warned

insights.claim: After NOA, Macmillan leadership has reportedly tried to integrate Google Gemini into publishing, and one editor called Gemini evaluations of agent submission letters useless; Macmillan says no directive to use Gemini in publishing was issued.
insights.speaker: Adam Morgan
insights.so_what: Enterprise switching from a niche vendor to a hyperscaler model is a pattern, but quality evidence at the user level is weak.

insights.claim: Staff at all of the Big Five publishers say executives are pushing AI tools even as Hachette, Macmillan, and Penguin Random House Verlagsgruppe sue leading AI companies for copyright infringement.
insights.speaker: Adam Morgan
insights.so_what: Publishers are both litigating against and adopting AI, a contradiction that may shape settlements and licensing terms.

insights.claim: At Penguin Random House, workers encouraged to use ChatGPT Enterprise say they avoid it whenever possible, though Hay House presented a slide deck calling it a core productivity, creativity, and collaboration tool.
insights.speaker: Adam Morgan
insights.so_what: Seat deployment by management may overstate real usage for OpenAI enterprise products.
insights.quote: It makes it harder for us to do our jobs,

insights.claim: Penguin Random House says its imprints have discretion over whether AI is appropriate for marketing, publicity and design workflows, and says it protects author IP and the role of human creativity.
insights.speaker: Adam Morgan
insights.so_what: Corporate positions are fragmented by imprint, so adoption policies are not uniform.

insights.claim: Bestselling Big Five authors, together selling more than 30 million copies, say AI use has harmed their relationships with publishers, including AI-hallucinated quotes in marketing copy and an inability to secure a no-AI promise in any contract.
insights.speaker: Adam Morgan
insights.so_what: Contract AI clauses are becoming a negotiation point; disclosure demand is rising.
insights.quote: I was gaslit on all of it,
insights.locator: Meanwhile, several bestselling Big Five authors

insights.claim: Cost-cutting layoffs at the Big Five are overloading editors, who authors say use Claude to produce marketing copy with little relation to the book and ask authors to write their own revision plans.
insights.speaker: Adam Morgan
insights.so_what: Headcount cuts drive AI adoption out of necessity, a labor-substitution dynamic with quality risk.

insights.claim: Bestselling authors with large readerships are considering self-publishing; Brandon Sanderson raised more than $15 million on Kickstarter to publish four books on his own in 2022.
insights.speaker: Adam Morgan
insights.so_what: Top-tier authors have proven direct-to-reader funding, threatening publisher leverage if trust erodes.
insights.locator: Bestselling authors who have already accumulated

insights.claim: One bestselling author argues that in trying to make authors obsolete with AI, publishers are rendering themselves obsolete.
insights.speaker: Adam Morgan
insights.so_what: Disintermediation risk cuts against the publishers' AI cost-saving narrative.
insights.quote: the publishers are rendering themselves obsolete.

insights.claim: Authors' baseline ask is disclosure of when and how publishers use AI, and some want the Big Five to agree shared principles on AI.
insights.speaker: Adam Morgan
insights.so_what: Disclosure standards are a likely first regulatory or contractual step.
insights.quote: The bare minimum we're asking for is disclosure,
insights.locator: All of the authors I spoke with
